passages.t: ‘No one alive is righteous before You’, and ‘Teach me to do Your will’
passages.happening:
The heading reads, “A Psalm of David” (verse 1). “O LORD, hear my prayer. In Your faithfulness, give ear to my plea; in Your righteousness, answer me” (verse 1). Then at once a confession. “Do not bring Your servant into judgment, for no one alive is righteous before You” (verse 2).

His enemy has crushed him and made him “dwell in darkness like those long since dead” (verse 3). “My spirit grows faint within me; my heart is dismayed inside me” (verse 4).

So he remembers. “I remember the days of old; I meditate on all Your works” (verse 5). “I stretch out my hands to You; my soul thirsts for You like a parched land” (verse 6).

Then a run of short prayers. “Answer me quickly, O LORD; my spirit fails” (verse 7). “Let me hear Your loving devotion in the morning, for I have put my trust in You” (verse 8). “Teach me to do Your will, for You are my God. May Your good Spirit lead me on level ground” (verse 10). “For the sake of Your name, O LORD, revive me” (verse 11).
passages.hearers:
Psalm 143 is the last of the seven ‘penitential psalms’, the prayers of sorrow for sin that the note on Psalm 130 describes.

Notice what the singer leans on. He does not ask God to answer because he, the singer, is good. He asks God to answer ‘in Your faithfulness’ and ‘in Your righteousness’ (verse 1). Then in verse 2 he admits that if God judged him by his record, he would fail, and so would everyone. His hope is in who God is.

‘A parched land’ (verse 6) is ground cracked by drought, thirsty for rain. The singer's soul is like that.

‘In the morning’ (verse 8) is the time of fresh hope after a long night. ‘Level ground’ (verse 10) is a path without stones to trip on.

Verse 10 is worth noticing. He does not only ask God to do his will for him. He asks God to teach him to do God's will.
passages.later: Paul echoes verse 2 when he writes, “Therefore no one will be justified in His sight by works of the law” (Romans 3:20). He says the same to the Galatians: “by works of the law no one will be justified” (Galatians 2:16). Both letters go on to speak of being put right with God through faith in Jesus Christ.
passages.hard:
Verse 12 asks God to ‘cut off my enemies’. It is a short example of the cursing prayers. The book page's part on the cursing psalms sets out how Christians read such lines, and no reading of them makes it right to harm anyone.

If ‘my spirit grows faint’ (verse 4) describes you now, please do not carry it alone. Tell someone you trust: a doctor, a pastor or a friend. The Find Help page on this site lists places to turn.
passages.asks:
Psalm 143 is a model of prayer from the bottom of a hard time. It confesses sin, it remembers what God has done, it reaches out to him, and it asks to be taught.

Which of its short prayers do you need today? ‘Answer me quickly.’ ‘Let me hear Your loving devotion in the morning.’ ‘Teach me to do Your will.’ Pick one and pray it.
